Abstract.AbstractText: Despite of the globally positive trends in epidemiology of tuberculosis, the ever increasing rates of drug-resistant strains are urging to introduce new antituberculars into clinical practice. Development of a new chemical entity from hit to marketed drug is an extremely time and resources consuming process with uncertain outcome. In this review we show that proper research of old drugs can be a very efficient way to new antituberculars. Firstly, we review the recent research on mechanism of action and molecular targets of first-line and second-line antituberculars and suggest how this knowledge can be used to design simple derivatives with improved properties. Secondly, we annotate old and known drugs from various pharmacodynamical groups as candidates for repurposing to become effective in combatting tuberculosis, either by direct effects on mycobacteria or by adjunct, host-directed therapy. Special attention is paid to elucidate the connection between repurposed drugs and new antituberculars in or close to clinical practise.
